---
**The Moon Is Leaving**

The moon is leaving. Not dramatically—no sudden darkness, no night it simply fails to rise—but leaving the way children leave home: a few centimeters a year, so slowly that no single generation can be blamed for not noticing.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable. The moon recedes from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters per year. We know this because we threw mirrors at the sky—mirrors left on the surface by Apollo astronauts—and bounce lasers off them, timing the round trip of light. We asked the sky to tell us the truth, and it did. 3.8 centimeters. Every year. The farewell is not a metaphor. It is a measurement.

No one chose this. It is just what happens when two bodies pull on each other for four and a half billion years. The moon's gravity raises tides, and those bulges of water drag slightly against the spinning Earth, slowing it—our days lengthen by about two thousandths of a second per century. Because the Earth is losing spin, the moon drifts outward to keep the books balanced. The Earth's loss of turn is the moon's gain of distance. Everything is conserved except closeness.

There is something almost domestic about it. The way a long marriage settles into a wider orbit. The way you can love something and still be pulled, slowly, out of reach of it.

Here is what I cannot stop thinking about: the total solar eclipse. It works only because of a coincidence so outrageous it feels like a gift left behind on purpose. The sun is about four hundred times wider than the moon and sits about four hundred times farther away, so from Earth they appear the same size—the moon a coin that exactly covers the sun, revealing the corona, the sun's atmosphere blooming around a black circle like a thought too large for the head that holds it.

But the moon is leaving, so one day—about six hundred million years from now, give or take—it will be too small to cover the sun completely. The corona will never again be fully revealed. The last total solar eclipse will occur, and no one will know it is the last, because that is how last things work. They do not announce themselves. Someone will stand in the moon's shadow, look up, see the corona, think it beautiful, and go home. And that will have been the last time, forever.

Six hundred million years is a long time. Complex animals have existed for only about that long. The whole career of bones, of eyes, of everything that crawled out of the sea and wrote poems about the moon—all of it fits inside the remaining tenure of the total eclipse. We are the midpoint creatures. Early enough to see it. Late enough to know why.

I keep trying to imagine a being, six hundred million years from now, reading our descriptions of totality: the sky going dark at noon, stars appearing, birds going silent, the cold that arrives with the shadow. That being will read it the way we read myths of a drowned island. A place that existed. A thing that happened. Not to them.

There is a version of grief that has no object. We know how to mourn a death, a demolished building. We do not know how to mourn a slowness. Across an entire human lifetime the moon withdraws by about three meters—invisible against a distance of 384,000 kilometers. No one has ever attended a funeral for the moon's departure. And yet it is the largest departure in the room.

My grandmother used to say, when something in the house broke and could not be fixed, "Well. It's the world getting wider." As a child I took her literally: the world expanding, everything on it drifting apart. It terrified me. Later I understood she meant it as a shrug, a way of filing loss under things that simply happen. But I have come back around to the literal reading. The world is getting wider. The distance between the Earth and the moon is a room whose walls are moving apart, and we are the furniture, and we cannot see the walls move.

What do you do with that? You look, I think. You look while the looking is good.

In 2024 a total solar eclipse crossed North America, and millions of people stood outside and looked up, and for a few minutes the traffic stopped and strangers gasped in unison, and everyone was pointed at the same thing. It is easy to be cynical about the crowds, the merchandising, the commemorative t-shirts. But underneath all that was the plain fact: people will stop their cars and stand in fields to see the moon cover the sun, knowing it is a coincidence of geometry, a temporary alignment, a thing that will end. That is not ignorance. That is attendance. That is showing up for the farewell party of a guest leaving at 3.8 centimeters a year, who will not be gone, in any way we can feel, for longer than animals have had eyes.

The moon is leaving, and the days are getting longer, and the eclipse is a finite resource, and none of this is urgent, which is why it matters, maybe. Everything urgent gets attended to. It is the slow departures that need someone to notice them at all.

Tonight, if it is clear, the moon will be up there—full, or waning, or a nail-paring of light; it is always something, never once in four and a half billion years has it been still. It is 384,400 kilometers away and 3.8 centimeters farther than it was last year at this time, and it will come up over the roofs the way it came up when my grandmother was a girl, when the tide pools held the first things sensitive to light. It will not rise for us in particular. It rises for no one. And still we look up, and still we point, and still someone, somewhere, says to someone else, look—the moon—and for a moment two people stand still under the slowest goodbye there is.
